Period schedule:

Total: 5 periods · 3h 45min

periods.activity_title: Reading Mrs. Jones's Stone Garden Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.19): fill eight blanks with exact words from the poem.
Let us discuss (p.19): three multiple-choice questions on tone, speaker, and rhyme scheme.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud, students following in their textbooks (p.17–18). A second unhurried reading invites one student per stanza to read aloud while the class listens for rhyme and rhythm.

Students individually complete the summary-fill task under “Let us read” (p.19), inserting exact words from the poem into eight blanks. Teacher circulates, prompting students to return to the poem text for each answer.

Class works through the three multiple-choice questions under “Let us discuss” (p.19) on tone, speaker, and rhyme scheme through open discussion. Teacher elicits reasons for each choice before confirming the answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the narrator-speaker with the poet Reginald Arkell; prompt them to distinguish the bemused neighbour-voice from the author. The poem’s refrain ‘My next-door neighbour, Mrs. Jones’ is a useful anchor for discussing how a repeated line creates tone. The context-fill sentences about the garden’s imagery (sundial, lily pond, crazy path) are not covered today and may be explored as self-study using p.20.

periods.activity_title: Unpacking Literary Devices and Situational Irony

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.20): identify examples of alliteration from the poem.
Let us think and reflect (p.20): identify the refrain that appears in each stanza.
Let us think and reflect (p.20): identify the lines that display situational irony.
Let us think and reflect (p.20): complete two sentences about the pun in the title ‘concrete’.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.20–21): read the first-stanza extract and answer four questions in writing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the poem’s three stanzas, reading the climactic final couplet aloud twice to set up today’s focus on literary devices. Students locate the stanza that features the flower conversation.

Students work in pairs to find alliteration in the poem and write examples; pairs share with the class. Teacher then elicits the refrain (‘My next-door neighbour, Mrs. Jones’) and discusses how repetition shapes the poem’s comic tone.

Whole-class discussion on situational irony: teacher reads the final couplet aloud and invites students to explain the gap between what the speaker expected and what happened. Students write the ironic lines in their notebooks.

Students complete the two sentences about the double meaning of ‘concrete’ in the title (p.20) individually. Teacher invites two students to share answers, confirming both the literal (stone) and symbolic (clear example) readings.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage often find alliteration only in initial-consonant pairs; prompt them to look beyond the first word — ‘small…stones’ and ‘pin…plants’ extend the search. The pun in ‘concrete’ is the poem’s sharpest wit, and spending a moment on it prepares students to appreciate the title’s layered meaning. The extract-analysis questions on p.20–21 are assigned for home reading so students can engage with them at their own pace.

periods.activity_title: Listening to the Rock Garden and Apologising with Care

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.23): answer five questions using one to three words from the Rock Garden presentation.
Let us speak (p.23–24): role-play informal apologies for four everyday situations using set phrases.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the Rock Garden context: a vast garden of sculptures made from waste, created by Nek Chand in Chandigarh. Students open notebooks and write the five question numbers, ready to fill in answers.

Teacher reads the Rock Garden transcript aloud at a measured pace (p.47), then reads it a second time while students write answers using one to three exact words. Teacher then reviews answers question by question with the class.

Teacher connects the poem’s garden world to the speaking activity: the speaker standing on Mrs. Jones’s flower would need to apologise. The class reads the informal-apology phrases from ‘Let us speak’ (p.23–24) aloud together.

Student pairs take turns role-playing informal apologies for situations (i)–(iv), using the listed phrases and practising responses. Teacher circulates, noting natural hesitation and prompting use of the full phrase set.

periods.teacher_notes: For the listening task, guard against students writing lengthy phrases rather than one-to-three-word answers; remind them the instruction requires brevity. During the role-play, some students may shy away from speaking assertively — the NCF pedagogy note on equal participation is worth applying here: nominate quieter students for the first exchange of each pair. The formal-apology task from ‘Let us speak’ (p.24) is rich material for extended practice and can be revisited independently.

periods.activity_title: Drafting a Notice and Exploring Word Families

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.25): draft a formal notice about the inauguration of the school’s Herb Garden.
Let us learn (p.22–23): create new words by replacing the first letter of ‘nice’ and ‘soil’.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a blank notice frame on the board, labelling the required components: organisation name, date, title, body, name, and signature. Students note the format in their notebooks.

Students draft their own formal notice for the Herb Garden inauguration (p.25), working individually. Teacher circulates and gives brief verbal feedback on third-person language, formal register, and completeness of required details.
Two or three volunteers read their notices aloud; the class checks each against the required components. Teacher highlights one strength and one improvement for each draft shared.

Students turn to ‘Let us learn’ (p.22–23) and complete the word-replacement table for ‘nice’ and ‘soil’ by changing the first letter. Teacher reviews answers quickly with the whole class using hints from the table.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently switch to first-person or informal language mid-notice; circulate and prompt a return to ‘third-person formal’ before the draft closes. The word-building activity with ‘nice’ and ‘soil’ connects directly to the poem’s language — students who enjoyed the pun in ‘concrete’ often engage enthusiastically with this wordplay. The synonym-matching and instrument-matching tasks from ‘Let us learn’ (p.21–22) are left as self-study for students who wish to extend their vocabulary work.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.25–26): research a popular local garden and prepare a short class presentation.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.26): collect fallen flowers and leaves; press and create a card or wall hanging at home.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly describes Amrit Udyan (p.25–26) as a model: its 15 acres, themed zones, and unique attractions. Students note down two or three features that make a garden ‘notable’, building a mental checklist for their own research.

In small groups, students brainstorm and note down what they know or can recall about a popular garden in their region — name, location, key features, why it is visited. Each group organises notes into a brief oral presentation structure: name, location, two highlights, and a personal connection.

Groups take turns delivering their short presentations to the class. Listeners note one thing they did not know about each garden. Teacher offers encouragement and highlights the variety of gardens represented — rock gardens, botanical gardens, heritage gardens.

Teacher introduces the pressed-flower homework activity (p.26): collect fallen flowers and leaves from the neighbourhood, press them under books, and create a card or wall hanging at home to bring back and display.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who cannot recall a specific garden by name can describe any green public space they know — the activity values observation and description over factual recall. The Amrit Udyan description on p.25–26 provides a ready scaffold if groups need a reference structure for their presentation. The pressed-flower project (p.26) takes a week of pressing time and is assigned as an at-home extension; it need not be assessed in class.

items.source_context: Reginald Arkell’s poem: Mrs. Jones’s stone garden, refrain, alliteration, situational irony in the final couplet, pun in the title ‘concrete’.
items.item_stem: Read the lines from the poem beginning “My next-door neighbour, Mrs. Jones,” that open every stanza. Which of the following best describes the effect of repeating this line at the start of each stanza?

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a comic, anchoring refrain that draws the reader back to Mrs. Jones as the subject throughout.

options.label: B
options.text: It is used to fill the syllable count of each stanza’s opening line.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the speaker admires Mrs. Jones and wants to highlight her name.

options.label: D
options.text: It signals a change in the speaker’s feelings about Mrs. Jones in each stanza.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests a misreading of the refrain as a shift marker rather than a structural and tonal anchor.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses ironic detachment with admiration; the speaker is bemused, not admiring.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reduces a deliberate literary choice to a mechanical constraint, ignoring the poem’s playful intent.

items.source_lo: Student reads and interprets a humorous poem by identifying tone, literary devices, and layers of meaning using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Reginald Arkell’s poem: Mrs. Jones’s stone garden, refrain, alliteration, situational irony in the final couplet, pun in the title ‘concrete’.
items.item_stem: The title of the poem is ‘A Concrete Example’. The word ‘concrete’ works on two levels in this poem. Identify both meanings and explain how each is connected to what happens in the poem. Support your answer with at least one detail from the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Literally, ‘concrete’ refers to the stones and hard surfaces that fill Mrs. Jones’s garden (the poem repeatedly mentions stones, a crazy path, a rockery). Figuratively, the title means a ‘clear’ or ‘definite’ example of how two people can perceive the same world very differently — illustrated by the speaker standing on Mrs. Jones’s treasured flower without noticing it.

items.source_context: Nek Chand’s Rock Garden: creation date, postage stamp feature, 40-acre area, three phases, waste-material sculptures, 5,000 border statues.
items.item_stem: Listen to the presentation about Nek Chand’s Rock Garden. Decide whether each of the following statements is true or false.

options.text: The Rock Garden covers an area of 50 acres.
The Rock Garden is divided into five distinct phases.
The Rock Garden was created by Nek Chand in 1957.
The Rock Garden was featured on an Indian postage stamp in 1983.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the presentation states Nek Chand created it in 1957.
2. False — the presentation states it covers 40 acres, not 50.
3. True — the presentation states it was featured on an Indian postage stamp in 1983.
4. False — the presentation states it is divided into three distinct phases, not five.

items.source_context: Nek Chand’s Rock Garden: creation date, postage stamp feature, 40-acre area, three phases, waste-material sculptures, 5,000 border statues.
items.item_stem: The Rock Garden presentation describes it as a place that “celebrates the best from waste.” Using details from the presentation, explain what kinds of waste materials were transformed into art and what this tells us about Nek Chand’s vision as a creator.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The presentation mentions terracotta pots, light fixtures, and broken toilet pots as examples of waste materials transformed into extraordinary sculptures and mosaic art. This shows that Nek Chand believed ordinary discarded objects could become works of art, celebrating creativity and resourcefulness.

items.item_stem: You borrowed your friend’s favourite book and accidentally left it on the bus. Role-play the conversation in which you apologise to your friend and your friend responds. Use informal language and at least two appropriate apology phrases.

expected_elements: Uses informal register consistently throughout the exchange.
Deploys at least two apology phrases naturally (e.g., ‘I’m really sorry’, ‘I didn’t mean to’).
Gives a brief, honest explanation of what happened.
Friend’s response is accepting and uses an appropriate informal reply.

items.source_lo: Student performs contextually appropriate spoken communication by selecting register and formulaic expressions using role-play as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Informal apology role-plays for four everyday situations using set phrases such as ‘I’m sorry about’ and ‘These things happen’.
items.item_stem: The speaker in the poem accidentally stood on Mrs. Jones’s treasured flower. Imagine you are the speaker and Mrs. Jones has just said, “You’re standing on it.” Role-play the apology you would give to Mrs. Jones, explaining why you did not notice the flower and expressing genuine regret. Then give your opinion: should the speaker have been more observant? Give one reason.

expected_elements: Opens with a sincere, contextually appropriate apology to Mrs. Jones.
Explains the reason for not noticing the flower (e.g., it was tiny, hidden among stones).
States a personal opinion on the speaker’s observational failure with one clear reason.
Maintains a polite, respectful tone appropriate to speaking to a neighbour.

items.source_context: Formal notice for the inauguration of a school Herb Garden, written in third-person formal language with required notice components.
items.item_stem: Your school’s Eco Club is organising a ‘Garden Awareness Walk’ around the school grounds for students of Grades 6 to 8. Draft a formal notice informing students about the event. Your notice must include: the name of the club, the date and time of the walk, the venue, a brief statement of purpose, and a contact name for queries. Write in third-person formal language and present your notice within a box.

expected_elements: Notice includes all five required components: club name, date/time, venue, purpose, contact.
Written entirely in third-person formal language with no colloquial expressions.
Notice is presented within a drawn or demarcated box.
Language is clear, concise, and free of personal pronouns.

items.source_context: Formal notice for the inauguration of a school Herb Garden, written in third-person formal language with required notice components.
items.item_stem: A neighbour like Mrs. Jones, who is passionate about her unusual stone garden, has inspired you to start a small community garden in your neighbourhood. Write a short notice for the community noticeboard inviting residents to a planning meeting for this garden. In your notice, include a brief persuasive sentence that explains why such a garden would benefit the community. Reflect in your answer: what can Mrs. Jones’s commitment to her garden teach the rest of us?

expected_elements: Follows notice format: heading, date, body with meeting details, and a sign-off.
Includes at least one persuasive sentence about community benefit of the garden.
Draws a genuine, reasoned connection to Mrs. Jones’s dedication as an inspiration.
Maintains formal register appropriate for a community noticeboard.

items.item_stem: Match each new word formed by changing the first letter of ‘nice’ (from the poem) with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A (new word) | Column B (meaning) |
|---|---|
| dice | to cut into small, even pieces |
| rice | a grain that is cooked and eaten as a staple food |
| mice | the plural of mouse |
| vice | a bad or immoral habit |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: dice – to cut into small, even pieces; rice – a grain cooked and eaten as a staple food; mice – the plural of mouse; vice – a bad or immoral habit.

answer_key.right: to cut into small, even pieces
a grain that is cooked and eaten as a staple food

items.source_lo: Student extends vocabulary by manipulating word forms and identifying relationships between words using a poem’s language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Word-building by replacing first letters of ‘nice’ and ‘soil’ to generate new words; meaning derived from definitional clues.
items.item_stem: The poem uses the word ‘soil’ as part of the garden world Mrs. Jones inhabits. By changing only the first letter of ‘soil’, four new words can be made. Choose the correct new word for each definition below and write a sentence using it in context.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The four words are: boil (to heat a liquid until it bubbles), toil (to work very hard), coil (a length of wire or rope wound in a circle), and foil (thin sheets used to wrap food). Accept any grammatically correct sentence that uses each word meaningfully.

items.item_stem: The poem ‘A Concrete Example’ celebrates an unusual garden created with passion and personal vision. Amrit Udyan in New Delhi is described in your textbook as a garden with multiple themed zones including a Tactile Garden, Bonsai section, and Herbal Garden. Write a paragraph of five to seven sentences describing a garden you have visited or know about in your region. Include: its name and location, two or three distinctive features, and one sentence explaining what makes it worth visiting.

expected_elements: Names the garden and gives its location clearly.
Describes two or three distinctive features with specific detail.
Explains what makes the garden worth visiting in one clear sentence.
Writing is in coherent paragraph form, five to seven sentences.

items.source_lo: Student connects a text’s themes to the wider world by researching and presenting real-world examples using project-work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Popular regional gardens researched and presented by students; Amrit Udyan with its themed zones as the model reference.
items.item_stem: Mrs. Jones’s garden in the poem is eccentric and personal — full of stones, tiny plants, and a sundial with a strange device. Amrit Udyan, by contrast, is a vast garden with carefully designed themed zones. Design a garden of your own on paper. Give your garden a name, describe at least three distinct zones or features, and explain in two to three sentences what theme or idea connects them. Then write a brief notice (four to five lines) inviting your classmates to visit your garden and experience its theme.

expected_elements: Garden has a clearly stated name and an overarching theme.
At least three distinct zones or features are described with specific detail.
A connecting idea or theme is articulated in two to three coherent sentences.
The invitation notice uses appropriate format and an engaging, welcoming tone.
